The chicks come out of it in three stages: at six months a bird carries about ten eggs, so three eggs per hatching is the natural hatching rate, and about six layings a year is the natural production rate, and both come from the same flock. The cock decides most of what comes out of the hen, and the reference says the cock decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy, so a poor cock will produce a lot of hens but poor chicks.

False. The ratio the 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference works on is one cock for about ten hens. One cock decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy, and he determines the number of eggs laid per laying. The hens lay about ten eggs a laying, and a brooding hen sits on twelve to fourteen eggs. With fewer hens you have fewer cocks to match, and the hens are more crowded, which is why the chick mortality is high. So the flock size is what decides the number of cocks, not how many chicks.
